title: The Proud Empire and the Remnant
overview: Isaiah condemns leaders who rob the poor, then declares that Assyria, used by the LORD to punish his people, will itself be cut down for its pride while a small remnant survives.

parts.label: Leaders who rob the weak (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Isaiah condemns officials who write laws and rulings that let them take from the poor, widows and orphans, though whether he means leaders in northern Israel or in Judah is unclear. Their wealth will not save them when disaster comes, and the repeated line about the raised hand, carried over from chapter 9, signals that judgment is not finished.

parts.label: Assyria, the LORD's tool (vv. 5-11)
parts.note: Isaiah pictures the empire of Assyria as a club the LORD uses to punish his own unfaithful people, though Assyria's king only means to conquer for himself. He brags that the cities he has already crushed, from Carchemish to Samaria, the northern capital of Israel, prove Jerusalem and its God will fall the same way.

parts.label: The boasting ax is judged (vv. 12-19)
parts.note: The king credits only his own strength and cleverness, boasting he took nations as easily as eggs from a nest, which Isaiah compares to an ax bragging that it swings the woodcutter. His army is pictured as a forest burned in one day until a child could count the trees left, and many readers link this image to the sudden collapse of the Assyrian force told in chapter 37, though this passage does not name that event.

parts.label: Only a remnant returns (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: The survivors will stop leaning on foreign powers and rely on the LORD, and the phrase 'a remnant will return' echoes the name of Isaiah's son in chapter 7. Christians read these verses through Paul, who quotes them in Romans 9 to speak of a faithful remnant within Israel.

parts.label: Do not fear Assyria (vv. 24-27)
parts.note: Jerusalem is told the beating will soon end, and the LORD will strike Assyria as he struck Midian in Gideon's day and Egypt at the sea. The yoke, a heavy wooden collar for oxen, will be broken, though the final phrase is obscure in the Hebrew and its exact sense is uncertain.

parts.label: The enemy at the gates (vv. 28-34)
parts.note: Town by town the poem tracks an army sweeping toward Jerusalem until it reaches Nob, close enough to shake its fist at the city, and scholars debate whether this traces a real route or is a dramatic picture. Then the LORD cuts down the towering forest like a woodcutter, an image of the proud invader suddenly felled.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the returning remnant refers mainly to survivors in Isaiah's own day, to Jewish followers of Jesus as Paul applies it, or to a future restoration of Israel still to come.
think: Can a person or nation be part of a larger story it never chose and still be fully responsible for its own motives?
